I need tips on how to pitch digital minimalism to my partner and his daughter. Hello! I need some tips, arguments, research and/or whatever to pitch digital minimalism to my partner and his daughter. Please, be kind, this is very difficult for me to talk about, and I'm doing this because I really need some support in all of this. I know that I can't force them to do anything, but I will give a little background. My step daughter is almost 15 and about a year ago it came to our knowledge that she's battling some mental health issues. She lives fulltime with her mom, and is living with us every other weekend and on school breaks. Now that she's over 13, she has more of a say in it all, so sometimes she's here more frequently and sometimes weeks can pass between visits. Anyway; she's glued to her phone, and always has been, basically. I came into their lives when she was 6 (turning 7 that same year), and it happened a lot that she used her dad's phone, mainly to watch youtube or play games. Whenever she was bored, the solution was often to let her have the phone; if not her dad always had to entertain her (she never had to play on her own). Even at that age she did show signs of anxiety, which I told her dad, but her mom dismissed it. Anyways, now that we're here, she's battling pretty severe mental health stuff like depression, severe anxiety and is doing a screening for ADHD and autism. I have battled mental health issues for most of my life, and from experience I know that social media doesn't affect us in a good way. I have done a light type of detox myself, and I feel so much better now compared to the last 10 years. In all of this with my step daughter, her psychologist have told her parents to not put any pressure on her, which they interpret as "let her do what she wants", but that's a whole other thing. But this leads to her having unlimited screen time basically, and whenever she "needs to rest", she's actually just doom scrolling. If I was her parent, I would want to give a more limited phone use a try, but I know I'm not her parent, so I can't. But I want to pitch the idea to my partner, so he might pitch it to his ex-wife. So, if you are a teen, or have a teen, or any other experience in how a social media detox have improved your mental health; I would LOVE to hear it.

Digital Dopamine Detox from my Worst Favorite Pastime. Hello, I've had a problem since probably age 6 or so with videogames. It appears I'm not the only one, so it's been heartening to find that I'm not alone. It's been enough that I was actually compelled to login to Reddit for the first time in forever. For years decades now I've known that this is a problem for me, that it's caused undue stress and anger on my person, that it's sublimated deeper feelings of loneliness and existential dread; that it's ruined relationships intimate and otherwise, and that most of all it's prevented me from finding my best self. I'm 36 now so to a decent degree that last one is permanent, but I need to prevent further damage and save myself - possibly anyone else that's reading this. Addiction isn't about chasing a high, but returning from a low. That's what the drug does, and that's largely why I played so much, to stave off daily stress whether that was in childhood (public school, friends moving away, the near-divorce of my parents), my 20s (major emotional and social fallout from my ex-fiance, unemployment stints), and my 30s (creeping existential dread, letting my body slowing down a bit). I've justified the gluttony by saying how much I love the narratives, how the social aspect has helped me meet some of my best friends, and how much the music has inspired me as a musician. I also justified it by saying that it didn't cost me money like alcohol or narcotics, so it was "better" for me by comparison. All of these things are at least a little true, which makes it even harder to permanently leave them behind. I do love that world, and it's come at a very high cost. Now for something a bit more hopeful: I've had stints where I've quit in the past and every time that I have my life has improved gradually and dramatically. As a teen, after destroying another game console out of anger, I found performance arts with poi and nunchaku. In college I was mostly quite disciplined and didn't game much, which led to successful study and taking up adult gymnastics. In my 20s, after losing another girlfriend (not from gaming but it didn't help) I took up what became my primary instrument with keys and synths, leading to live performance from there. In my 30s with job prospects drying up and another mouse and controller destroyed, I quit to study computer programming deeply and while I ultimately didn't land there I now have a real career that I'm quite happy with. Every time I've quit my life has improved dramatically, so I know the positives of what can happen. So now for today, it's a Monday at the end of the month. I have a loving wife and a solid network of friends, and at the end of this week I'm moving into what will be my first house. It will need work, but it's magnificent. There's a wonderful garden to maintain, I want to build a workout room for gymnastics strength training, then another room for a music studio for recording and creating, and then an entertainment room for hosting people, and more. I'm also due to start a family, her and I are in our mid-30s so we don't have a lot of time left to try. I was brought here after Googling "how to remove gaming content from YouTube" since that also hasn't helped me. In-between typing this I uninstalled Heroic from my computer, and I gave up custody of my Steam account the last time I quit. I haven't owned a console in over a decade. All of this to say that I'm trying, and that my life depends on doing so. I know a lot of the answer, as I was taught multiple times from insurance sales to sports coaching, is to create your schedule and honor your schedule one day at a time - the latter is the hard part. If I can do this for my day job where other people make a schedule for me then I can damn well do this for myself at home. I want to make this house the setting from which I can try to build again, built around all the interests I've listed above and new ones like maintaining a large garden. I thank you if you've read this far. This has been a nice meditative release for me, to get my sins in writing so to speak. I need to make this last, to live up to being my best self. I'll die trying if I have to, because this can't go on any longer. I hope your day treats you and yours well out there, and if this post meant anything to you I'd love to know your thoughts as well. Cheers

Does a digital detox lower measurable stress? The evidence is thinner than the hype. I’ve heard everyone saying how good you feel after doing a digital detox, but no-one really talks about what actually happens behind-the-scenes. We mostly rely on self-reported results — so there aren’t many examples of real objective data being used to validate the effects of a detox. That’s why I found this little-known pilot study from 2018 particularly interesting. It involved people wearing a wristband to measure things like “skin conductance” which is a physiological measure of stress. Basically they got to wear an electronic bracelet for two weeks — the first week using their mobiles as normal, then the next week going through a digital detox. Researchers saw stress levels drop during the second week. This was obviously a pretty small scale study though, given its designation as a ‘pilot’ study – and also with its relatively low sample size, the authors do say “further research would be useful”. That’s probably necessary, because we haven’t been able to establish much consistent evidence yet. Just recently I read another paper describing some randomised trials showing the inconsistency in smartphone abstinence intervention research — suggesting perhaps even the effectiveness of complete abstinence isn’t certain. A quick search shows there was a trial registering for this test to put a cap of two hours per day during three weeks (the other version uses questionnaires to assess perceived stress rather than looking at things like cortisol). So maybe that’ll be interesting once the results are available — I’d love to see what the real impact of a detox really is on actual physiological stress indicators. Have you done one? What were your experiences? Anything you can actually measure?
